sections.title: Marriage
sections.lead: Allah could have made us complete and alone; instead He made hearts that settle only in another’s company. Marriage in Islam is a sign of God before it is a contract: a shelter built from sakina, the settling calm, mawadda, tender love, and rahma, mercy. Enter it with reverence, and leave your selfishness at the door like a pair of shoes.

ps: The Qur’an does not introduce marriage with law but with wonder: He created for you, from yourselves, mates, that you may find rest in them. Sakina, the settling calm, is the stated purpose; mawadda, tender love, and rahma, mercy, are the materials Allah Himself places between two strangers. Whoever thinks marriage is merely paperwork has not yet read the verse that calls it a sign.

The Prophet ﷺ urged the young who are able toward marriage, naming it a guard for the eyes and a fortress for chastity. A beloved narration, received warmly by scholars though it sits outside the strictest collections, calls marriage half of a person’s religion. However its chain is weighed, its meaning is proven daily: most of the soul’s battles, patience, desire, anger, generosity, are fought and won at home.

refs.note: rest, love, and mercy between spouses
the young urged to marry, guarding chastity

ps: Islam refuses a marriage of one creditor and one debtor. The Qur’an says of spouses that women have rights like those over them, according to what is honorable, and it commands husbands: live with them in kindness. Ma’ruf, honorable dealing, is the shared law of the house; neither love nor authority cancels it.

In his farewell sermon the Prophet ﷺ set the two duties side by side: you have rights over your wives, and they have rights over you, provision and clothing given generously, dignity kept whole. If you would know your standing with Allah in marriage, do not count what you are owed. Count what you have paid of what you owe.

refs.note: rights mirrored in honorable measure
live with them in kindness
farewell sermon names mutual rights of spouses

ps: Asked what the Messenger of Allah ﷺ did inside his house, Aisha did not describe a man waited upon. She said that he was in the service of his family, and when the prayer was called he rose and went out to it. Other sound reports fill in the picture: he patched his garment, mended his sandals, milked the sheep. The most honored man alive ﷺ did chores, and heaven recorded it.

He raced Aisha on a journey and she won; years later, when she had grown heavier, he outran her, laughed, and said, “this one is for that one.” He drank from her cup, setting his lips where hers had been, and he joked with his household while insisting that even his jokes carried only truth. Tenderness was not beneath his rank ﷺ. It cannot be beneath yours.

refs.note: he served his family until prayer time
he raced Aisha, playful on a journey
he drank from the place of her lips
he patched garments and milked the sheep

teachings.t: Speech is the weather of the house
ps: A good word is written as sadaqa, charity, and nowhere is that charity more due than across your own table. The Prophet ﷺ said that gentleness does not enter a thing except that it adorns it, and is not torn from a thing except that it disfigures it. A marriage is made of ten thousand sentences; their tone is the climate your family lives in.

When a man asked him ﷺ what a wife is owed, he answered in plain domestic verbs: feed her as you feed yourself, clothe her as you clothe yourself, do not strike the face, do not revile her, and do not shun her except within the home. Notice that insult stands beside violence in that list. The tongue can bruise what the hand never touched.

refs.note: a good word counts as charity
gentleness adorns everything it enters
feed her, clothe her, never revile or degrade

ps: The Qur’an makes the mahr, the wedding gift, her property outright, given graciously and never clawed back. It likewise leaves in her hand whatever she earns or owns; marriage joins hearts, not her wallet. A husband provides not as a favor to be invoiced but as a duty he was honored with.

The Prophet ﷺ said the best dinar a man spends is the dinar spent on his family, and that whoever provides for his household seeking Allah’s reward has given charity. So budget together, conceal nothing, and let fairness be visible enough that no one has to ask for it. Money quarrels are rarely about money; they are about whether mercy has a line in the budget.

refs.note: the mahr is hers, given graciously
each keeps a share of earnings
the best dinar is spent on family

ps: Every marriage knows storms; revelation does not pretend otherwise, it builds lightning rods. If a wife fears cruelty or coldness, the Qur’an says, let the two make terms of settlement, for settlement is best. If the rift widens, it commands arbiters, one from his people and one from hers, and promises that when both truly want repair, Allah Himself causes accord between them.

The Prophet ﷺ answered a man who asked for counsel with two words, repeated until they rang: do not become angry. He taught that the strong one is not the wrestler but the one who owns himself when anger rises, and he prescribed seeking refuge in Allah from Shaytan in that hot moment. Sit down, lower your voice, delay the verdict. You cannot repair a house while it is on fire.

refs.note: settlement between spouses is best
arbiters from both families, Allah grants accord
his repeated counsel: do not become angry

ps: Surah an-Nisa 4:34 names men qawwamun, those charged with standing over the family’s care and provision, then sketches steps for a grave breach of the marriage: counsel, then distance in the bed, then a third word, daraba, that readers have wrestled with for fourteen centuries. Some classical jurists read it as a token gesture so slight it must leave no mark and cause no harm; others read it as a restriction meant to end the beatings of pre-Islamic Arabia; some later scholars read the verse as pointing toward separation. Honesty requires saying plainly: the readings differ.

What does not differ is the Prophet’s ﷺ own record. Aisha testified that he never once struck a woman or a servant, and when men who hit their wives were mentioned to him he said that such men are not the best of you. Whoever seeks Allah through this verse while ignoring the man ﷺ sent to embody it has misread both. The Qur’an gave marriage arbiters and honorable exits; it gave no one a license for cruelty.

refs.note: responsibility, and a long-debated word
he never struck a woman or servant
those who strike are not your best

ps: The Prophet ﷺ said: let no believing man despise a believing woman, for if one trait in her displeases him, another will please him. This is the sunnah of the unlisted faults: you married a whole person, and you do not get to keep only the chapters you like. Whoever catalogues a spouse’s failures builds, entry by entry, the case against his own happiness.

And the Qur’an closes the ledger from above: let them pardon and overlook; do you not love that Allah should forgive you? It even warns that spouses and children can become your trial, then commands in the same breath: if you pardon and overlook and forgive, then surely Allah is Forgiving, Merciful. Forgiveness in marriage is not one grand treaty. It is a small daily amnesty, renewed before sleep.

refs.note: dislike one trait, another will please
pardon, as you hope for pardon
forgive family, Allah forgives you

ps: The deepest intimacy two believers can share is a direction. The Prophet ﷺ asked Allah’s mercy for the man who rises in the night to pray and wakes his wife, and for the woman who rises and wakes her husband, each sprinkling water on the other’s face when sleep argues back. A couple that has stood side by side before Allah at night holds a bond no daytime argument easily breaks.

Make the Qur’an’s own prayer your household motto: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and descendants the coolness of eyes, and make us a model for the God-fearing. Fast a Monday together, give charity from one hand, keep a shared list of duas, supplications you are both carrying. You are not only building a home. You are rehearsing Paradise, where the righteous enter with their spouses and are made glad.

refs.note: mercy on spouses who wake each other to pray
spouses and children, coolness of eyes

practice: Thank your spouse tonight for one specific thing, named out loud.
Do one act of service at home daily, the way he ﷺ mended and served.
When anger rises, sit down, lower your voice, and seek refuge in Allah.
Never reopen a fault you have already forgiven.
Agree on money openly: what is shared, what is hers, what is his.
Once a week, pray two rak’as together and make one dua for your marriage.
Say the love in plain words; do not make your spouse guess.

sections.title: Intimacy
sections.ar: المَوَدَّة, al-mawadda, tender love between spouses
sections.lead: Islam does not blush at the body; it dignifies it. What passes between spouses behind a closed door is counted as worship, guarded as a trust, and rewarded as charity. The tone of revelation here is neither crude nor cold, and a believer’s tone should match it.

ps: The companions were startled when the Prophet ﷺ said that in the intimacy of each of you there is sadaqa, charity. Does one of us satisfy his desire, they asked, and receive a reward for it? He answered with a question: if it were placed in the forbidden, would there not be sin? So when it is placed in the lawful, there is reward.

This is the quiet revolution of the Islamic marriage: desire is not a shameful appetite to be endured but a trust that becomes worship by where and how it is spent. You do not leave your religion at that door. You bring it in, and it blesses what it finds.

refs.note: in lawful intimacy there is charity

ps: The Qur’an chose its metaphor with care: they are a garment for you and you are a garment for them. A garment rests directly on the skin, conceals what should be concealed, warms, adorns, and is chosen to fit. Revealed concerning the nights of Ramadan, the verse folds desire itself into the language of tenderness.

So let nothing in that room be rushed or careless. The scholars of law wrote plainly what shyness often hides: a spouse should be attentive to the other’s share of joy, not merely his own. Unhurried kindness, a word before a touch, warmth before need: that is the garment worn best.

refs.note: spouses described as garments for each other

teachings.t: The secret that stays in the room
ps: The Prophet ﷺ named among the worst of people in rank before Allah on the Day of Resurrection the one who is intimate with his wife, and she with him, and then spreads her secret. The bedroom is a house within the house, and its door does not open outward. What was given to you in trust was never yours to narrate.

This covers the joke to friends, the complaint to relatives, the hint dropped online. Modesty here is not prudishness; it is loyalty. A spouse who knows the door is sealed can be fully present behind it, and that safety is itself a form of love.

refs.note: worst of people spreads the bedroom’s secrets

ps: Within marriage each spouse holds a real claim on the other’s closeness, and the Prophet ﷺ said it directly to a man drowning in voluntary worship: your wife has a right over you. Neither husband nor wife should treat warmth as a favor to be rationed, for coldness starves what the covenant was built to feed.

But a claim in Islam is never a license to wound: the Prophet ﷺ ruled that there is no harming and no reciprocating harm. So ask, and answer generously; meet illness, exhaustion, and grief with patience, not pressure. Tenderness demanded at any cost stops being tenderness. Offered freely, it heals what the day has broken.

refs.note: your wife has a right over you
no harming and no reciprocating harm

ps: Purity is half of faith, and the sunnah carries it into intimacy: washing, sweetness of breath and body, the ghusl, the full ritual bath that closes the act, the fragrance he ﷺ loved. Preparing yourself for your spouse is not vanity; it is a courtesy of love, and husband and wife are equally owed it.

The same fire that warms a hearth burns the house down when it escapes. The Qur’an praises those who guard their desire except with their spouses, and commands: do not even approach zina, unlawful intimacy, for it is a road that begins long before the act. Lower the gaze outside, and bring your desire home. What is kept is blessed, and what leaks is lost.

refs.note: purification is half of faith
desire guarded, except with spouses
do not approach unlawful intimacy

practice: Guard the bedroom’s secrets completely; tell no friend, ever.
Come to each other unhurried; give the word before the touch.
Keep yourself clean and pleasant for your spouse, as you would be met.
Ask gently, answer generously, and never coerce or punish with distance.
Begin with the name of Allah and intend mercy for each other.
Lower your gaze all day, and bring your desire home.

sections.title: Children
sections.ar: التَّرْبِيَة, at-tarbiya, the patient raising of souls
sections.lead: A child is not an accessory to your life; a child is a soul on loan, arriving with rights already written. The Prophet ﷺ kissed his grandchildren in public and carried a granddaughter through the prayer itself. Raising children in Islam is slow mercy with a long horizon: dua before they arrive, justice while they grow, dignity as they rise past you.

teachings.t: Ask for them before they arrive
ps: The prophets begged for children the way the poor beg for bread. Zakariyya, peace be upon him, prayed: My Lord, grant me from Yourself a good offspring. The servants of the Merciful plead: Our Lord, grant us from our spouses and descendants the coolness of eyes. A child prayed for is received differently from a child merely acquired.

The sunnah plants dua, supplication, at the very moment of conception: in the name of Allah; O Allah, keep Shaytan from us, and keep Shaytan from what You grant us. Begin your parenthood before the pregnancy test, in the dark, with your hands raised. What you ask Allah to shape, you will be gentler shaping.

refs.note: Zakariyya begs for good offspring
children as coolness of eyes
dua at conception, shielding from Shaytan

teachings.t: A name they can stand in
ps: Your child will hear one word more than any other for a lifetime, and the sunnah treats that word as a gift owed. The Prophet ﷺ said the most beloved of names to Allah are Abdullah and Abdur-Rahman, names that bow, and he changed ugly names into beautiful ones, renaming a woman called Asiya, disobedient, as Jamila, beautiful.

On the seventh day come the aqiqa, the sacrifice of welcome, the shaving of the soft hair, and the naming. Choose a name your child can carry into every room without flinching: one that will sound right in the mouth of a teacher, a spouse, and the caller on the Day when names are called.

refs.note: most beloved names, Abdullah and Abdur-Rahman
seventh day: sacrifice, shaving, naming
he changed a harsh name to beautiful

ps: A chief of the desert watched the Prophet ﷺ kiss his grandson and boasted that he had ten children and had never kissed one. The answer came without flattery: whoever does not show mercy will not be shown mercy. He ﷺ carried his granddaughter Umama on his shoulder in the prayer itself, setting her down when he bowed and lifting her when he rose.

He ﷺ also said that whoever shows no mercy to our young and no honor to our old is not of us. Affection withheld is not discipline; it is debt. Kiss your children, hold them, let them interrupt your importance sometimes. When a grandchild climbed onto his back in prostration, he stayed down, unhurried, until the child was done.

refs.note: no mercy shown, none received
he prayed carrying his granddaughter
not of us without mercy for the young

teachings.t: One scale for all of them
ps: A father came asking the Prophet ﷺ to witness a gift he had made to one son. He asked: have you given the like of it to every one of your children? The man said no. He answered: fear Allah and be just between your children, and he refused to witness the gift, calling the imbalance by its true name.

Children keep books of what they were given, and longer books of what their siblings were given. Favoritism plants the crooked seed that grew between the sons of Yaqub. Equal gifts, equal kisses, equal patience; and where needs truly differ, explain openly, so fairness is seen as well as done.

refs.note: fear Allah, be just between your children

ps: The sunnah gives salah, the prayer, a seven-year runway: instruct your children in it at seven, and hold them firmly to it by ten. Seven years of watching you pray, praying beside you, being praised for a crooked sujud; the firmness comes only after long apprenticeship. Allah told His Prophet ﷺ: enjoin prayer upon your family and persevere in it yourself. The order of that verse is the method.

So teach it the way you taught walking: applaud the wobble, steady the fall, never mock. A child shamed at the prayer mat learns shame, not prayer. Your own unhurried salah in the middle of the house, seen year after year, is the strongest sermon your children will ever attend.

refs.note: teach prayer at seven, firmly by ten
enjoin prayer on family, persevere

ps: The Prophet ﷺ rode with a boy seated behind him and handed him not a lecture but a treasure: young one, be mindful of Allah and He will guard you; when you ask, ask Allah. Anas served him from boyhood into youth, ten full years, and swore he never once heard uff, nor a why did you do it, nor a why did you not.

When Ibrahim, peace be upon him, received the heaviest command a father ever carried, he still turned to his son and asked: look, what do you see? Consultation is the language the almost-grown hear as love. Command less, ask more; correct in private, honor in public. The teenager you dignify today is the adult who will still sit with you tomorrow.

refs.note: the young taught trust in Allah
ten years of service, never scolded
Ibrahim consults his son first

teachings.t: Daughters, a screen from the Fire
ps: A mother came to Aisha with two daughters and nothing to give them; Aisha found three dates. The woman handed each girl a date, and when they wanted more, she split her own between them and ate nothing. When the Prophet ﷺ heard of it he said: whoever is tested with daughters and treats them excellently, they will be a screen for him from the Fire.

He ﷺ also joined two fingers and said that whoever raises two girls until they come of age will stand with him like this on the Day of Resurrection. A world that once buried its daughters was taught to see Paradise standing behind them. Let your daughter never wonder whether a son was wished in her place. She is not a consolation; she is a shield.

refs.note: daughters raised well screen from the Fire
raise two girls, stand beside him

practice: Make dua for your children daily, by name, even before they exist.
Give each child a name to be proud of in every room.
Kiss your children today and tell them plainly that you love them.
Keep gifts and praise even between siblings; explain any difference openly.
Teach prayer with praise for seven years before firmness at ten.
Consult your teenager before deciding for them; correct privately, honor publicly.
Celebrate your daughters aloud, and spend on them gladly.

sections.title: Parents
sections.ar: بِرُّ الوالِدَيْن, birr al-walidayn, devoted goodness to parents
sections.lead: In the Qur’an, kindness to parents is decreed in the same breath as the worship of Allah Himself, one verse holding both. Whatever they were, they carried you when you could not carry yourself. Now, for the grown child, a door of Paradise stands open inside an ordinary house, wearing a mother’s face and a father’s slowing hands.

ps: Your Lord has decreed that you worship none but Him, and to parents, excellence. The verse does not pause between the two clauses, and neither may you. Then it descends into detail small enough to fit a kitchen: if one or both reach old age with you, do not say to them uff, the smallest syllable of irritation, do not repel them, and speak to them a noble word.

Then it teaches the grown child a posture: lower to them the wing of humility out of mercy, and say, My Lord, have mercy on them as they raised me when I was small. You cannot repay the nights you cost them; that debt was designed to be unpayable. What Allah asks instead is a lifetime of gentleness, with the interest paid in dua.

refs.note: worship Him; excellence to parents; no uff
the wing of humility, the dua
thank Allah, and thank your parents

ps: A man asked the Prophet ﷺ: who among people most deserves my finest companionship? He said, your mother. The man asked, then who? Your mother. Then who? Your mother. Then who? Your father. Three parts of the answer went to the one who carried, delivered, and nursed, weakness upon weakness, before you could thank anyone.

When another man came eager for the battlefield, the Prophet ﷺ asked whether his mother was living, then told him: stay with her, for Paradise is at her feet. Rank with Allah waits in unglamorous places, beside a stove, at a sickbed, on the far end of a patient phone call. Go where the Paradise is.

refs.note: your mother, three times, then father
stay with her; Paradise at her feet

ps: May his nose be rubbed in the dust, said the Prophet ﷺ, and he repeated it three times: the one who finds his parents in old age, one or both, and does not enter Paradise through them. Notice the grammar of the rebuke. The failure is not merely unkindness; it is a squandered entrance. Their old age is not your burden. It is your door.

The years when parents shrink, repeat themselves, and need what infants need are the years when the reward compounds. You are watching your own future in slow motion; serve it with the tenderness you will one day hope to receive. The child who was once cleaned without complaint learns, at last, to clean without complaint.

refs.note: disgrace: aged parents found, Paradise missed

teachings.t: When they do not share your faith
ps: Islam does not cancel the debt to parents even at the widest divide. The Qur’an rules that if they strive to make you worship other than Allah, you do not obey, and then, in the very same verse: but accompany them in this world with honorable kindness. Belief is not owed to them; beauty of conduct still is.

Asma bint Abi Bakr asked the Prophet ﷺ about her mother, still an idolater, who had come to her seeking help. He said: maintain the bond with your mother. And Allah declares that He does not forbid kindness and justice toward those who never fought your faith. Your excellence toward a non-Muslim parent is not a compromise of your religion. It is your religion.

refs.note: no obedience in shirk; kind company
keep ties with your idolater mother
kindness and justice remain due

ps: Death ends their needs but not your duty, and mercifully, not your opportunities. The Prophet ﷺ said that when a person dies, his deeds end except three, and one of them is a righteous child who prays for him. Your istighfar, your pleading for their forgiveness, your charity given in their name, your pilgrimage performed for them: these travel where you cannot.

He ﷺ also called it among the finest of all devotion that a man keep warm the friendships his father loved. So visit their friends, settle their promises, and hold the relatives who exist in your life only through them. Grief that turns into deeds is grief the dead receive as gifts.

refs.note: a righteous child’s prayer keeps benefiting
honor the friends your father loved

ps: The Prophet ﷺ said that the pleasure of the Lord lies in the pleasure of the parent, and His displeasure in theirs. This is no charter for parental tyranny, for no creature may be obeyed in disobedience to the Creator. It is a compass: across the wide field of lawful choices, lean toward what makes them glad.

And remember that a parent’s dua is counted among the supplications that are not turned away. You walk through life inside the weather of their prayers, for you or against you. The phone call that softens an old heart tonight may quietly be rewriting your fortunes in the unseen.

refs.note: the Lord’s pleasure in the parent’s
a parent’s supplication is answered

practice: Call or visit your parents today; bring warmth, not just duty.
Strike uff and every sharp sigh from your voice with them.
Give your mother the first call, the first visit, the first ease.
If they are aging, serve their needs as your door to Paradise.
If they are not Muslim, honor them beautifully all the same.
After they die, pray for them by name, give charity for them, and visit their friends.

sections.title: Kinship
sections.ar: صِلَةُ الرَّحِم, silat ar-rahim, joining the womb-bond
sections.lead: Your relatives are not an accident of birth; they are a bond Allah named after His own mercy. The rahim, the womb-bond, clings to the Throne itself and pleads to be joined. To keep those ties while they are warm is good manners. To keep them after they turn cold is worship.

teachings.t: A bond named from the Merciful
ps: The Qur’an opens its great chapter on family with a command: fear Allah, through whom you ask of one another, and the wombs. The Prophet ﷺ related that Allah said of the rahim, the womb-bond: I am ar-Rahman, the Most Merciful, and I have derived its name from My own; whoever joins it, I join him, and whoever severs it, I sever him.

He ﷺ also described the rahim as clinging to the Throne, repeating that same plea like a plaintiff who never leaves the court. Family ties in Islam are not sentimentality. They are a covenant with one of God’s Names woven through it, and Heaven keeps the account.

refs.note: fear Allah, and the wombs
the rahim named from ar-Rahman
the rahim clings to the Throne

ps: The Prophet ﷺ said: whoever loves that his provision be expanded and his lifespan extended, let him maintain his ties of kinship. Scholars have turned the promise over for centuries: blessing poured into wealth, blessing poured into years, a name that goes on living after death, and the plainest reading besides, that it simply works as stated.

Notice what the hadith prescribes for the two anxieties that govern modern life, money and time. Not a scheme and not a supplement, but an aunt called, a cousin visited, a grandfather’s hand kissed. The believer’s web of kin is not networking. It is rizq, provision, wearing family clothes.

refs.note: kinship ties expand provision and lifespan

teachings.t: Join the one who cuts you
ps: The Prophet ﷺ drew the line sharply: the wasil, the true joiner of kin, is not the one who merely reciprocates; the true joiner is the one who, when his kin cut him off, reaches out and joins them. Reciprocity is accounting. Silat ar-rahim, the joining of the bond, is charity that keeps flowing uphill.

A man complained: I give to relatives who wrong me, I join those who sever me, I stay patient while they are harsh. He ﷺ answered: if it is as you say, it is as though you feed them hot ashes, and a helper from Allah will remain with you as long as you continue. Their coldness is their record. Your outstretched hand is yours.

refs.note: true joining is not mere reciprocation
patience with harsh kin brings Allah’s support

ps: The Prophet ﷺ taught that charity given to the poor is one charity, but given to a relative in need it is two: sadaqa, and sila, the joining of the bond. Islam has no patience for the strange generosity that funds distant causes while a struggling cousin watches in silence from the family gathering.

The Qur’an lists the near of kin first in nearly every roll call of giving: Allah commands justice, excellence, and giving to relatives. Begin your generosity at the nearest door and work outward. No one holds more claim on your surplus than the people who hold claim on your salam.

refs.note: to kin it is charity twice over
justice, excellence, giving to relatives

teachings.t: Justice in what you leave behind
ps: Inheritance is the last conversation you will ever have with your family, and Allah wrote its script Himself: for men a share of what parents and close relatives leave, and for women a share, an obligation decreed. The fixed portions of the Qur’an are not suggestions; the verses that carry them end with a warning of Fire for those who transgress His limits.

The Prophet ﷺ closed the loopholes in a sentence: Allah has given every rightful heir his right. No scheming a daughter out of her portion, no secret transfers to a favorite, no punishing an estranged son from the grave. Write your will while you are healthy, disclose it without drama, and leave your family your justice as their final memory of you.

refs.note: men and women hold decreed shares
every rightful heir given his right

practice: List your relatives and their needs; work through the list monthly.
Call or visit one relative weekly, starting with the least easy.
Answer a relative’s coldness with an invitation, not a tally.
Give struggling kin before strangers; the reward counts twice.
Write a just will now, and let no heir be wronged.
Never let a year close on an unhealed family rift.

sections.title: Friendship
sections.lead: You become what sits beside you. Islam takes friendship seriously because the heart is porous; it slowly absorbs the religion, the speech, and the appetites of its companions. So choose souls that pull you upward, love them for the sake of Allah, and tell them so while you both can hear it.

ps: The Prophet ﷺ said: a person is upon the religion of his khalil, his closest friend, so let each of you look carefully at whom he takes as an intimate. The narration, graded hasan, sound, by the scholars, states a law of the heart that experience keeps confirming. Closeness is transfer; habits migrate quietly between people who love each other.

The Qur’an shows the far end of careless company: close friends, on that Day, will be enemies to one another, except the God-fearing. Audit your inner circle the way you audit your food. You are not told to abandon every struggling soul, but the seats nearest your heart are appointments. Fill them with people whose presence makes Allah easier to remember.

refs.note: a person follows his close friend’s religion
that Day, friends become enemies

ps: Among the seven whom Allah will shade on the Day when there is no shade but His are two who loved each other for His sake, meeting upon it and parting upon it. Another man once traveled to see a brother in a distant town, and an angel was posted on his road to tell him: Allah loves you as you love him.

And the Prophet ﷺ made the love speakable: when a man loves his brother, let him tell him that he loves him. Believers do not ration affection as if saying it shrank the giver. Say it plainly and mean it for His sake: I love you for the sake of Allah. That sentence, said truly, is a deed with shade in it.

refs.note: two who loved for Allah, shaded
an angel meets the visiting friend
tell your brother that you love him

teachings.t: The mirror that tells the truth
ps: The religion itself, said the Prophet ﷺ, is nasiha, sincere counsel. And he said the believer is the mirror of the believer: a mirror shows you the mark on your face quietly, at close range, without announcing it to the street, and it does not flatter. A friend who only applauds you is a portrait, not a mirror.

So give counsel in private, with a soft voice and a clean motive, and receive it without mounting a defense. Umar is remembered for saying: may Allah have mercy on the one who gifts me my faults. Keep one friend brave enough to tell you the truth, and be that friend for someone. Flattery is abandonment wearing perfume.

refs.note: the religion is sincere counsel
the believer is the believer’s mirror

ps: The Qur’an legislates against the small cruelties that pass as humor: let no people ridicule another people, for perhaps they are better than them; do not insult one another; do not wound each other with nicknames. Then it goes deeper still: shun much suspicion, do not spy, and do not backbite, which it pictures as eating the flesh of a dead brother.

Friendship in Islam is a protected space where a person’s honor stays safe in his absence, especially in his absence. The joke that costs your friend his dignity is priced too high; retire the sting and keep the laughter. The Prophet ﷺ joked with his companions and spoke, even in jest, nothing but truth.

refs.note: no ridicule, insults, wounding nicknames
no suspicion, spying, or backbiting

ps: The Prophet ﷺ numbered the rights of one Muslim over another: return the greeting, answer the invitation, give counsel when it is sought, answer the sneeze, follow the funeral, and visit the sick. He said that the one who visits a sick person remains in the harvest of Paradise, gathering its fruit until he returns home.

In a hadith qudsi, Allah says: son of Adam, I was sick and you did not visit Me; had you visited My servant, you would have found Me with him. Friendship is proven in hospital corridors, at gravesides, in the awkward silence of another’s grief. Anyone can attend a wedding. Attend the hard days, and Allah will attend yours.

refs.note: six rights, among them visiting the sick
the visitor stays in Paradise’s harvest
qudsi: you would find Me with him

practice: Choose close friends whose company makes Allah easier to remember.
Tell a friend today, in plain words, that you love him for Allah’s sake.
Give counsel privately and gently; praise generously in public.
Retire every joke that costs a friend his dignity.
Visit your sick friend this week and sit close.
Guard your friend’s honor in his absence as your own.

sections.title: Neighbors and Guests
sections.ar: الجِوار, al-jiwar, the sacred bond of neighborhood
sections.lead: Jibril kept urging the Prophet ﷺ about the neighbor until he thought neighbors would be written into each other’s wills. Your faith is audited at the fence line: in the smell of your cooking, the volume of your night, the safety people feel behind the nearest wall. From there Islam widens the circle outward, to the guest, the stranger, and the shared road.

ps: The Prophet ﷺ said: Jibril kept counseling me about the neighbor until I thought he would assign him a share of inheritance. Revelation returned to the subject so relentlessly that the Prophet ﷺ expected the neighbor to enter family law. That is the rank Islam gives to the person you did not choose, who simply lives beside you.

Your neighbor holds claims no contract records: the greeting, help in hardship, discretion about whatever you inevitably see and hear, congratulation at the right door and condolence at the same one. Learn the names behind the nearest walls. On a street where a Muslim lives, no one should feel unwatched over.

refs.note: Jibril nearly made neighbors into heirs

ps: By Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe; by Allah, he does not believe. They asked: who, O Messenger of Allah ﷺ? He said: the one whose neighbor is not safe from his harms. In another wording, such a person does not enter Paradise. Islam measures creed at the property line.

Harm wears ordinary clothes: noise at sleeping hours, the blocked path, a tongue that carries what the window showed, the slow menace of contempt. Before you polish the worship that faces Allah, secure the conduct that faces your neighbor. The Prophet ﷺ tied the first to the second and never untied them.

refs.note: no faith while the neighbor fears harm
no Paradise while the neighbor is unsafe

ps: O Abu Dharr, said the Prophet ﷺ, when you cook broth, increase its water, and look to your neighbors. The instruction is almost comically small, one ladle of water, and that is its genius: neighborliness is built from increments too cheap to excuse skipping. He also told the believing women never to despise a neighbor’s gift, even a sheep’s trotter.

Do not wait until you can host a feast. Send the extra plate while it is hot, the dates from your travel, the soup on the day someone behind that wall is ill. Small kindnesses, repeated, do what grand gestures cannot: they make your presence on the street feel like shade.

refs.note: add water to the broth, share it
despise no gift, even a trotter

ps: Whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day, let him honor his guest. The Prophet ﷺ then set out the measures of a generous chivalry: the prize of welcome is a day and a night of your best, and hospitality is three days; whatever follows is charity. The guest, in Islam, arrives carrying rights of his own.

Honor lives in details: the better portion served first, the bed you would accept yourself, the unhurried face that lets a visitor forget he is one. There is courtesy on the guest’s side too, not to overstay until welcome becomes weight. Keep a house that strangers bless after they leave it.

refs.note: honor the guest; hospitality is three days

teachings.t: Greet the face you do not know
ps: Asked which Islam is best, the Prophet ﷺ answered: that you feed food, and offer the salam, the greeting of peace, to those you know and those you do not know. When Abdullah ibn Salam, a rabbi of Madinah, first studied his face, the words he heard him ﷺ proclaiming were these: spread the salam, feed food, join the ties of kin, pray in the night while people sleep, and enter Paradise in peace.

The greeting is a small treaty offered to strangers, and your face is part of its seal. He ﷺ said: do not belittle any good deed, even meeting your brother with a bright face, and he counted your smile for your brother as sadaqa, charity. Cities are softened one salam at a time. Be the reason a stranger revises his opinion of the believers.

refs.note: feed food, greet known and unknown
spread peace, feed, pray, enter Paradise
meet your brother with a bright face

ps: The companions loved to sit out in the open street, and the Prophet ﷺ did not forbid the gathering; he billed it. If you must sit there, he said, then give the road its right: lowering the gaze, withholding harm, returning the greeting, enjoining what is good and forbidding what is wrong. Even the ground you idle on has a claim against you.

He ﷺ also counted the removal of what harms from people’s path as a branch of faith itself. Our roads now include the feeds and threads where we sit in public; the same rights apply there. Guard the eyes, harm no passerby, answer the greeting, stand for good, and clear the way. Be, in every kind of street, the one who makes passage safer.

refs.note: the sitting place owes the road’s rights
removing harm from the road is faith

practice: Learn the names of the neighbors on both sides of your door.
When you cook, make extra and carry a plate next door.
Greet first, with a full salam and a bright face.
Host your guest with your best for a day, and welcome for three.
Keep your noise, your trash, and your temper on your side of the wall.
Give the road its rights: lower your gaze, clear harm, return greetings.
